/WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 214 PM CDT Mon Sep 7 2026

By Wednesday, the combination of continued southwesterly flow and 
moisture pooling ahead of an advancing cold front is expected to 
boost dewpoints back into the low/mid 70s, with some compressional 
warming also possible ahead of the front. This leads to actual 
temperatures once again in the mid/upper 90s but with much more 
noticeable humidity, and current ensemble mean forecasts suggest 
that areas that stay south of the front will see heat index values 
in the 105-110 degree range Wednesday afternoon. The key point of 
contention, then, is how quickly the front will push through the 
area, as this will determine how much of our area will see another 
round of headline-worthy heat. Since this is a one-day thing (or 
perhaps two for parts of central MO) and because we are still 48 
hours away, we will hold off on issuing any heat headlines (most 
likely in the form an Advisory) until we can narrow this down over 
the next 24 hours. However, we suspect that at least some areas 
along and south of I-70 are more likely than not to have some form 
of heat headline by this time tomorrow. In fact, some areas north of 
I-70 will likely be cooler Wednesday than Thursday thanks to the 
front, and perhaps some lingering showers and cloud debris from 
lingering nocturnal convection along our northern fringes. 

During afternoon, the focus shifts to the passage of a slow-moving 
cold front, which will be driven south by a shortwave moving 
through the upper Mississippi Valley and Great Lakes. As 
mentioned in the short term discussion above, the combination of
prolonged moisture advection and pooling ahead of the front 
will boost precipitable water values to at least the 95th 
percentile of climatology (2+ inches) in a narrow corridor as it
moves through Missouri and Illinois. Modest instability is also
expected to develop, with roughly 750-1500 J/kg of MU CAPE on 
either side of the boundary. Competing with this instability
will be what appears to be a strong-warm sector cap, though, 
which limits our confidence in surface-based storms developing 
in the warm sector. Not only this, but dynamic forcing remains 
relatively weak along the front, and this limits our confidence 
in storms firing anywhere but right along and behind it. Still, 
there is enough shear, moisture, and instability to support some
organized updrafts capable of locally heavy rain and occasional
downbursts, although the latter may be limited if storms remain
elevated. 

Not only this, but storm motions are likely to move nearly 
parallel to the boundary itself, and although outflow should 
keep the front moving south, some limited training of storms is 
possible and we can't rule out a few streaks of heavier rain 
(1-3 inches). Rain rates will likely be quite high in the 
stronger cores, so these amounts shouldn't be too difficult to 
achieve even if the coverage is limited. Fortunately, the 
flooding threat should be rather limited, as a lack of recent 
rain should help the soil soak most of this (much needed) rain 
up. Showers and thunderstorms should slowly move south between 
late Wednesday afternoon and early Thursday morning, with the 
most widespread coverage overnight. 

From Thursday onward, confidence in the day-to-day details drops 
considerably. On the one hand, we do expect a significant 
temperature drop from Wednesday to Thursday, with ensemble 
temperature forecasts near seasonal averages Thursday afternoon with 
minimal spread. There is also likely to be a lull in precipitation 
during the day Thursday in the wake of the activity the previous 
night. Beyond that, a slowly building ridge across the Mississippi 
Valley and eastern CONUS is more likely than not to drive a gradual 
warming trend back to at least slightly above average, with 
continued uncertainty regarding the strength/position of the ridge. 
Not only does this impact the timing and magnitude of rising 
temperatures, but also our exposure to additional shortwaves and 
rounds of showers/storms. Once such shortwave seems to have a 
bit more broad support among ensembles late Friday/early 
Saturday, with current precipitation probabilities of 30-50%. At
the moment, this represents the next best opportunity for 
additional rain beyond Wednesday.
